identity.title: Fever onset temporally linked to a new drug (with rash/relative bradycardia)

technique.how: Build a dated medication timeline (start/stop of every agent, including antibiotics, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, heparin) against the fever curve. Look for fever beginning after a new drug, a patient who looks relatively well despite high temperatures, a pulse lower than expected for the temperature, rash or eosinophilia, and defervescence within about 72 h of stopping the suspect drug.
technique.prerequisites: Complete medication reconciliation; other infectious and non-infectious causes actively sought and excluded.
technique.contraindications: Do not stop essential drugs (e.g., antimicrobials for a proven infection, immunosuppressants) without a risk-benefit assessment.

interpretation.positive_finding: Fever temporally following a new drug, with no alternative source and resolution after withdrawal, supports drug fever; antibacterials (beta-lactams, vancomycin, rifampicin, aminoglycosides) are the commonest culprits and median onset is about 2 days but the lag is highly variable.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of rash, eosinophilia or relative bradycardia does not argue against drug fever: these accompaniments were found in only a minority of cases in the largest series. Persistence of fever more than a few days after stopping the suspect drug argues against the diagnosis.
interpretation.pitfalls: Textbook features (relative bradycardia, rash, eosinophilia, characteristic fever pattern) are absent in most cases; drug fever is a diagnosis of exclusion and infection must be ruled out first. Rechallenge reproduces fever and is usually inappropriate.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: stop the suspect drug (substitute if needed), expect defervescence within ~72 h, continue infection work-up. Negative: keep searching for occult infection, thrombosis or malignancy.

sources.citation: Mackowiak PA, LeMaistre CF. Drug fever: a critical appraisal of conventional concepts. An analysis of 51 episodes in two Dallas hospitals and 97 episodes reported in the English literature. Annals of internal medicine. 1987.
Vodovar D, LeBeller C, Mégarbane B et al. Drug Fever: a descriptive cohort study from the French national pharmacovigilance database. Drug safety. 2012.

Cunha BA. The diagnostic significance of relative bradycardia in infectious disease. Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases. 2001.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not attribute fever to a drug in a neutropenic, septic or haemodynamically unstable patient until infection has been excluded; do not withdraw life-sustaining drugs on this basis alone.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Fever with rash, mucosal involvement, facial oedema, eosinophilia or organ dysfunction may be DRESS/SJS: stop the drug immediately and escalate.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: No interobserver data; attribution relies on causality assessment (e.g., Naranjo criteria) which is inherently subjective.

extraction_notes: No diagnostic-accuracy study (sensitivity/specificity/LR) of a temporal drug-fever history against a reference standard exists; the entity is defined by exclusion and dechallenge, so status is not_quantified. Descriptive evidence only: Mackowiak 1987 (PMID 3565971; 51 hospital episodes plus 97 literature episodes) found 'relative bradycardia in a minority of cases', 'a highly variable lag time between the initiation of the offending agent and the onset of fever', and 'an infrequent association with either rash or eosinophilia' (Abstract); the exact proportions are in the full text, which is not accessible via PMC. Vodovar 2012 (PMID 22830618; 167 pharmacovigilance cases without skin reaction): 'Median time [interquartile range] from drug administration to fever onset was 2 days [1.0-10.5]' and 'Drug rechallenge was performed (38.0%), resulting in recurrence of DF in all cases' (Abstract, Results); antibacterials most frequently implicated, e.g. amikacin PRR 39.6 [23.6, 69.0], vancomycin 4.0 [1.4, 11.5] (Abstract, Results). Cunha 2001 (PMID 11284920) is a narrative review of relative bradycardia with no abstract on PubMed and is cited as consensus only. The 72-hour defervescence expectation is conventional teaching (unverified recall).
